analysis.reasoning: The CLI-side parser `proto2num` (src/tool_paramhlp.c:288-403) correctly computes a zero bitmask for `--proto -all,-http` (lines 366-367 clear all bits via `-all`, then `-http` clears an already-cleared bit). However, it then converts that zero bitmask back to an empty string (lines 390-400: the loop emits nothing, `strdup("")` returns a non-NULL empty string, and `PARAM_OK` is returned). The bug hinges on how libcurl interprets that empty string when it arrives via `CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR`. If libcurl treats an empty string as "all protocols allowed" (the default) instead of "no protocols allowed", the claim holds. The provided `lib/setopt.c` snippet ends before the `CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS_STR`/`CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS_STR` cases, so I cannot verify the libcurl-side parsing behavior.
key_lines: src/tool_paramhlp.c:366-367 - deny action clears bits: `val &= ~(pp->bit)` for 'all' clears everything
src/tool_paramhlp.c:390-400 - zero bitmask produces empty string: loop body skipped, `*ostr = strdup(obuf)` where obuf is ""
lib/url.c:1862 - protocol check uses `data->set.allowed_protocols & p->protocol`; if allowed_protocols ends up non-zero, HTTP succeeds

None of the listed exclusions (memory leaks, never-ending transfers, API misuse, local attackers, experiments, URL inconsistencies, command-line arguments, busy-loops, file saving, command-line tricks, terminal output, NULL dereferences) cover this report. analysis.reasoning: The bug is in lib/vtls/gtls.c lines 1323-1395. The condition `if(gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked(session, 0) == 0)` at line 1324 is inverted. According to the report and GnuTLS behavior, `gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked()` returns non-zero when an OCSP stapling response EXISTS (any status: GOOD, REVOKED, UNAUTHORIZED, UNKNOWN). The current code only enters the detailed status-checking block (lines 1331-1394) when the function returns 0 (i.e., NO response). When a response exists (function returns non-zero), the `else` branch at line 1396-1397 executes, logging "server certificate status verification OK" and skipping all status validation. This means UNAUTHORIZED (6), UNKNOWN, and any non-REVOKED status are treated as success. The REVOKED case is caught earlier by `gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2()` at line 1286 (which sets GNUTLS_CERT_INVALID_OCSP_STATUS), but all other non-GOOD statuses bypass verification entirely.

findings.text: The buggy code is in lib/vtls/gtls.c (not gnutls.c as reported; near-miss filename). Lines 1323-1395 contain the OCSP verification logic.

Line 1324: `if(gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked(session, 0) == 0)` is inverted. Per GnuTLS docs, this function returns non-zero when ANY OCSP stapling response exists (GOOD, REVOKED, UNAUTHORIZED, UNKNOWN). The code only enters detailed validation when the function returns 0 (NO response).

Lines 1396-1397 (else branch): when a response EXISTS (function returns non-zero), curl logs "server certificate status verification OK" and skips all status validation. This treats UNAUTHORIZED (6), UNKNOWN, and any non-REVOKED status as success.
Line 1286: `gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2()` catches REVOKED status via GNUTLS_CERT_INVALID_OCSP_STATUS and fails correctly. The bug affects only non-REVOKED failure statuses.

Call chain: gtls_connect_common (line 1728) -> gtls_verifyserver -> Curl_gtls_verifyserver (line 1323). The buggy block is reached when config->verifystatus is true (set by --cert-status option). No pre-validation of OCSP response occurs.
No sandbox reproduction was run. The test site https://ocsp4test.sytes.net:4433 (claimed to return UNAUTHORIZED status) was not tested against the code.
The GnuTLS manual URL cited discusses session initialization defaults but does not document the return-value semantics of gnutls_ocsp_status_request_is_checked().

scope.reason: The report describes a TLS certificate verification bypass in the mbedTLS backend when connecting via IP address. None of the policy's 'Not security issues' categories (small memory leaks, never-ending transfers, not practically possible, API misuse, local attackers, experiments, URL inconsistencies, visible command line arguments, busy-loops, saving files, tricking users, terminal output) cover this type of cryptographic verification failure. analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability exists in the mbedTLS backend. In `mbed_connect_step1` (lib/vtls/mbedtls.c), `mbedtls_ssl_set_hostname` is called only when a client certificate/key is configured (`ssl_config->key || ssl_config->key_blob` at line 685 in caller context). When called, it passes `connssl->peer.sni` which is NULL for IP addresses (lib/vtls/vtls.c:1597-1613 sets `peer->sni` only for `CURL_SSL_PEER_DNS`). mbedTLS treats a NULL hostname as disabling certificate name verification. For typical HTTPS connections without client certs, the function is never called at all, skipping verification entirely. Other backends (wolfSSL at lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:768-770) correctly fall back to `peer->hostname` when `peer->sni` is NULL. The comment at lib/vtls/mbedtls.c:687-689 acknowledges the function must be used even for IP addresses, but the code does not implement this.

verdict.headline: curl with mbedTLS skips certificate hostname verification when connecting via IP address because mbedtls_ssl_set_hostname is only called when SNI is configured, and SNI is not set for IP addresses.

findings.text: Static analysis confirms the vulnerability in lib/vtls/mbedtls.c: mbedtls_ssl_set_hostname is called only when client cert/key is configured (line 685 context), and when called it passes connssl->peer.sni which is NULL for IP addresses (lib/vtls/vtls.c:1597-1613). mbedTLS treats NULL hostname as disabling certificate name verification.
Other TLS backends in curl (wolfSSL at lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:768-770) correctly fall back to peer->hostname when peer->sni is NULL, but mbedTLS backend does not.
Code comment at lib/vtls/mbedtls.c:687-689 acknowledges 'even if curl connects to a host specified as an IP address, this function must be used' but the code does not implement this fallback.
CVE-2016-3739 documents the exact same issue in curl's history; the fix was later reverted/reintroduced per the cited commits.
Mbed TLS documentation confirms hostname verification is skipped when SNI is not set (e.g., IP address connections), confirming this is a usage gap in curl's integration.

The exact code snippets quoted in the report (if(connssl->peer.sni) {...} and Curl_ssl_peer_init block) were not found verbatim in the current codebase, suggesting the report may reference a slightly different version or the reporter approximated the code.
No sandbox reproduction was executed to verify the exploit works end-to-end against a real server.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report. Static analysis of the current codebase (commit fb3c251) confirms the vulnerability: in lib/vtls/mbedtls.c, mbedtls_ssl_set_hostname is only invoked when a client certificate/key is present, and it receives connssl->peer.sni which is NULL for IP addresses (set only for DNS names in lib/vtls/vtls.c:1597-1613). mbedTLS treats a NULL hostname as disabling certificate name verification entirely. Other backends (wolfSSL) correctly fall back to peer->hostname. The code comment at mbedtls.c:687-689 acknowledges this requirement but the fallback is not implemented. This matches the historical CVE-2016-3739. A fix would need to call mbedtls_ssl_set_hostname with peer->hostname when sni is NULL, for all connections (not only when client certs are configured). We were unable to run a sandbox reproduction; if you can provide a minimal test case or confirm the behavior against a controlled server, that would help finalize the fix.

scope.quote: If a malicious server can trigger a NULL dereference in curl or otherwise cause curl to crash (and nothing worse), chances are big that we do not consider that a security problem.
scope.reason: The report describes a buffer overread (out-of-bounds read) that reads past a non-NUL-terminated certificate buffer into adjacent memory, which could leak sensitive data. analysis.reasoning:
The bug is real and exploitable. In GTime2str (lib/vtls/x509asn1.c:484-548), when a GeneralizedTime string contains a '.' or ',' followed immediately by a non-digit (no fractional seconds), the following occurs:

1. Line 517: `tzp = fracp` (both point to '.' or ',')
2. Line 520: `fracp++` (now points after '.'/','), but `tzp` still points to '.'/','
3. Lines 521-523: do-while loop runs once: `tzp++` makes `tzp` point to the same char as `fracp` (the timezone indicator). Loop exits because `*tzp` is not a digit.
4. Line 525: `fracl = tzp - fracp - 1` = -1. Since `fracl` is `size_t` (line 490), this wraps to SIZE_MAX.
5. Line 525 loop condition `fracl && fracp[fracl - 1] == '0'` has undefined behavior (massive out-of-bounds read). Compiler optimizes the loop away, leaving `fracl` = SIZE_MAX.
6. Line 546: `(int)fracl` passed as precision to `%.*s` in format string. Cast to `int` yields -1.
7. In lib/mprintf.c:878-883, precision -1 triggers `strlen(fracp)`. Since `fracp == tzp` (both point to timezone char in certificate buffer), this is `strlen(tzp)`.
8. The certificate buffer is not NUL-terminated (it's a length-delimited ASN.1 element), so `strlen` reads past `end` into adjacent stack/heap memory.

The ASan report confirms: crash in `strlen` called from `formatf` -> `Curl_dyn_vprintf` -> `Curl_dyn_vaddf` -> `Curl_dyn_addf` -> `GTime2str:542`, reading 4471 bytes past a stack buffer.

analysis.reasoning: The bug occurs in `hsts_add` (lib/hsts.c:413-452) when loading cache entries. When a cache line starts with '.' (indicating `includeSubDomains`), `hsts_add` calls `Curl_hsts(h, p, TRUE)` at line 439 to check for existing entries. `Curl_hsts` with `subdomain=TRUE` matches any existing entry that has `includeSubDomains=TRUE` and whose host is a suffix of the lookup name with a preceding dot (lib/hsts.c:277-285). When loading `.hsts.badssl.com`, this incorrectly matches the existing `.badssl.com` entry (host="badssl.com") because "hsts.badssl.com" ends with ".badssl.com" (offs=5, hostname[4]=='.', strncasecompare matches). Line 443-445 then updates the matched parent entry's expiration to the child's value instead of creating a new child entry. This corrupts the in-memory cache: the parent's expiration becomes the child's, and the child entry is never created. On save, only the parent entry exists with the child's old expiration. The next request creates a new child entry, resulting in the parent having the child's previous expiration and the child having a new one.

title: freeing stack buffer in utf8asn1str
headline: The function utf8asn1str() calls free() on a stack-allocated buffer (char buf[4]) when processing a malicious TLS certificate, which is undefined behavior and reachable during certinfo extraction.

ref.why: commit linked in the report (04739054cdac)

claims.summary: The function utf8asn1str calls free() on a stack-allocated buffer (char buf[4]), which is undefined behavior and can lead to heap corruption and control-flow hijacking.
repro_steps: The attacker sets up a malicious server with a TLS certificate that triggers the invalid free() in utf8asn1str
An application using libcurl connects to the server and during the connect() phase parses the invalid certificate
The stack address is put into the freelist of the allocator
The attacker causes the stack address to be returned by a malloc() call and used to store attacker data

scope.reason: The report describes a memory safety bug (calling free() on a stack-allocated buffer) triggerable by a malicious TLS certificate during the handshake. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not include this class of issue, and no other section explicitly excludes it.

analysis.reasoning: The function `utf8asn1str` declares `char buf[4]` on the stack at line 378. At line 397, when the decoded code point `wc >= 0x00200000`, it calls `free(buf)`. This is undefined behavior: `free()` must only be called on pointers returned by heap allocators. The condition `wc >= 0x00200000` occurs when the input ASN.1 string (type BMP_STRING/UTF-16 or UNIVERSAL_STRING/UTF-32) contains a code point beyond the valid Unicode maximum (U+10FFFF). A malicious TLS certificate can supply such a string. The call chain is: TLS handshake → `Curl_ossl_verifyhost`/`wolfssl_connect_step2` → `Curl_extract_certinfo` → `ASN1tostr` → `utf8asn1str`. The attacker controls the certificate content, so they can trigger the invalid `free()`.

analysis.test_plan: Create a malicious TLS certificate with a subjectAltName of type GENERAL_NAME containing a BMPString (UTF-16BE) or UniversalString (UTF-32BE) where a code point >= 0x200000 (e.g., 0x00200000 encoded as 4 bytes: 0x00 0x20 0x00 0x00 for UTF-32, or surrogate pair for UTF-16). Run curl against a server presenting this certificate with CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=1 and CURLOPT_CERTINFO=1 (to force certinfo extraction). Observe crash or heap corruption under glibc without free() pointer validation (e.g., Ubuntu 18.04).

callers.why: Passes `elem->beg, elem->end` directly from parsed ASN.1 element; no validation of code point ranges. The element data comes from the certificate.

analysis.reasoning: The bug is in `override_login` (lib/url.c:2654-2765). When a redirect creates a new connection for a different host, `override_login` calls `Curl_parsenetrc` for the new host. If the .netrc entry for the redirect target (or 'default') provides a login but no password, `parsenetrc` sets `*userp` to the new login but leaves `*passwdp` NULL (lib/netrc.c:245-254). After `parsenetrc` returns, the fallback logic at lib/url.c:2752-2761 sees `data->state.aptr.passwd` (the password from the previous request, which was obtained via netrc for the original host) and, because `!*passwdp` is true, copies that old password into the new connection via `*passwdp = strdup(data->state.aptr.passwd)`. Similarly, if the .netrc entry provides neither login nor password, both fall back to the previous request's credentials at lib/url.c:2735-2744 and 2752-2761. The code does not clear `data->state.aptr` before calling `Curl_parsenetrc` for the new host, so credentials from the original host leak to the redirect target.

scope.reason: The report describes a double-close race condition on an eventfd file descriptor in multi-threaded libcurl code that could allow file descriptor hijacking and redirection of sensitive data. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain any category that clearly covers this type of vulnerability (race condition / fd reuse / use-after-close). The listed exclusions address memory leaks, never-ending transfers, API misuse, local attackers, experiments, URL parsing, command-line arguments, busy-loops, file saving, social engineering, terminal escapes, and NULL dereferences/crashes — none of which match a multi-threaded fd double-close leading to fd hijacking. Therefore the policy does not clearly place this report out of scope.

analysis.reasoning: The report describes a double-close of an eventfd file descriptor in multi-threaded libcurl code. The provided source shows `curl_multi_cleanup` (lib/multi.c:3155-3161) closes `wakeup_pair[0]` unconditionally but only closes `wakeup_pair[1]` when `USE_EVENTFD` is NOT defined. This suggests `wakeup_pair[0]` and `wakeup_pair[1]` may be the same fd when `USE_EVENTFD` is defined (eventfd is a single fd for both read/write), but the cleanup code only closes index 0. However, the actual `wakeup_create` and `wakeup_close` implementations are not in the provided files, so I cannot confirm whether the same fd is stored in both array slots, whether `wakeup_close` is idempotent, or whether a race between `curl_multi_wakeup` (which writes to `wakeup_pair[1]` from another thread) and `curl_multi_cleanup` could cause a double-close. The `GOOD_MULTI_HANDLE` guard and `multi->magic = 0` (line 3144) prevent double-cleanup of the same multi handle, but the report's race involves three distinct threads (curl, writer, listener) where the OS reuses the fd number after the first close. To evaluate this, I need the wakeup implementation.

investigation.summary: The report claims a double-close of an eventfd file descriptor in multi-threaded libcurl. However, the code shows that under USE_EVENTFD (which is enabled on 64-bit architectures), wakeup_create calls Curl_eventfd which creates a single eventfd stored in wakeup_pair[0], while wakeup_pair[1] is initialized to CURL_SOCKET_BAD and never changed. The cleanup code at lib/multi.c:3155-3161 only closes wakeup_pair[0] when USE_EVENTFD is defined (the second close is guarded by #if !defined(USE_EVENTFD)). Since wakeup_pair[1] remains CURL_SOCKET_BAD, there is no double-close of the same file descriptor. The race condition described in the report cannot occur because the second close never happens for eventfd.

analysis.reasoning: The provided parsenetrc() snippet (lib/netrc.c:97-296) is incomplete — the function continues to line 339 but the critical loop-exit and return logic is not shown. The visible parsing state machine has a plausible flaw: when 'default' is encountered in NOTHING state (line 227-230), it sets state=HOSTVALID and retcode=NETRC_SUCCESS but does NOT reset the `found`, `our_login`, or `keyword` variables (unlike the 'machine' keyword at line 220-222 which does reset them). If the unseen portion of the function uses `found` to decide whether to return the currently-stored login/password, a non-matching host could incorrectly inherit credentials from a preceding 'machine' section. However, the visible code frees login/password at line 223-225 when 'machine' is parsed, so the variables would be NULL unless `specific_login` is true (which the report says it is not). The override_login caller (lib/url.c:2702-2729) treats any ret==0 as success and sets conn->bits.netrc=TRUE, causing those credentials to be sent even on redirect (lib/http.c:792-799). Without the rest of parsenetrc (lines 297-339) we cannot confirm whether the function returns the stale pointers or correctly returns NULL.

Static analysis shows parsenetrc() at lib/netrc.c:227-230 sets success state for 'default' keyword without resetting found/our_login/keyword variables, unlike 'machine' keyword handling at lines 220-225 which does reset them.

The provided parsenetrc() snippet ends at line 296 but the function continues to line 339; the loop exit, 'out' label, and final *loginp/*passwordp assignment are not visible, so we cannot confirm whether stale credentials are returned for non-matching hosts.
override_login() at lib/url.c:2706-2729 treats any ret==0 from Curl_parsenetrc as success and sets conn->bits.netrc=TRUE, which causes credentials to be sent on redirect per lib/http.c:792-799.
No sandbox reproduction was attempted; the reporter claims the issue persists in curl 8.11.1 but this was not verified.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the report. CVE-2024-11053 is a known netrc credential leak during redirects. The static analysis shows a plausible gap in the 'default' keyword handling in parsenetrc() (lib/netrc.c:227-230) where state variables are not reset like they are for 'machine'. However, the remainder of parsenetrc() (lines 297-339) is not in the provided snippet, so we cannot confirm whether the function correctly returns NULL credentials for non-matching hosts or incorrectly returns stale pointers. The caller override_login() trusts any zero return code. Could you provide a minimal .netrc file and curl command that demonstrates the leak against a test server, or confirm whether you have tested with curl 8.12.0 (which includes the fix via commit 9fce2c5)?

findings.claim: The fix for CVE-2024-11053 is incomplete; netrc default credentials are incorrectly used for hosts not explicitly configured, causing sensitive information disclosure.

investigation.summary: The parsenetrc function in lib/netrc.c has a logic flaw: when 'default' is encountered in NOTHING state (line 227-230), it sets state=HOSTVALID and retcode=NETRC_SUCCESS but does NOT reset the 'found', 'our_login', or 'keyword' variables (unlike 'machine' at line 220-225 which does reset them and frees credentials). This means if a 'machine a.com' block with credentials precedes 'default' (with no credentials), parsing for host 'b.com' will enter HOSTVALID state via 'default' with stale 'found' and 'our_login' values from the previous 'machine' block. The function then returns NETRC_SUCCESS (retcode=0) with the previous host's credentials still in login/password pointers. The override_login caller in lib/url.c:2706 treats ret==0 as success and sets conn->bits.netrc=TRUE, causing those credentials to be sent to b.com. This is a bypass of the CVE-2024-11053 fix which only addressed the HOSTVALID state 'default' case (line 291-296). A sandbox reproduction is needed to confirm the leak.

analysis.analysis: Based on the provided curl source code, the IDN/punycode handling occurs in lib/idn.c (win32_idn_to_ascii using Windows IdnToAscii API) and lib/urlapi.c (curl_url_get calling Curl_idn_encode/decode). verdict.headline: Report describes a plausible stack-buffer overread in the Apple IDN backend (mac_idn_to_ascii) when ICU's uidna_nameToASCII_UTF8 fills the 256-byte buffer exactly, leaving it non-NUL-terminated; the code path exists only when built with USE_APPLE_IDN and has not been reproduced or verified against the actual source at the cited commit.

findings.text: ICU's uidna_nameToASCII_UTF8 is documented to not NUL-terminate when output length equals buffer capacity (ICU source: ustring.cpp:1437), matching the report's root-cause claim.

The provided evidence does not include lib/idn.c from commit 58772b0e; static_analysis notes 'Full lib/idn.c (Curl_idn_encode, Curl_idn_decode, IDN_MAX_LENGTH, IDN backends)' as missing, so the existence and exact content of mac_idn_to_ascii at that commit is unverified.
Reproduction was not run; the PoC requires building with -DUSE_APPLE_IDN -licuuc, which was not tested in the sandbox.
The proposed patch mirrors PHP's defensive handling of the same ICU function (PHP idn.c:69), adding a length check and explicit NUL-termination.

The vulnerability is correctly scoped: it only affects builds that enable the Apple IDN backend (USE_APPLE_IDN), requires attacker-controlled URL input, and results in an information leak rather than code execution.

investigation.summary: The vulnerability is confirmed in the curl source at commit 58772b0e082e: mac_idn_to_ascii() calls uidna_nameToASCII_UTF8() with a 256-byte buffer but ignores the return value (destination string length). ICU documentation confirms the function returns the destination string length. If the encoded output exactly fills the 256-byte buffer, ICU does not NUL-terminate (standard ICU behavior for capacity-limited string functions), leaving buffer non-NUL-terminated. The subsequent strdup(buffer) then reads past the buffer boundary. This code path is only active when built with USE_APPLE_IDN. A sandbox reproduction with ASAN is needed to confirm the exploitability and impact.

scope.reason: The report describes an integer overflow leading to heap corruption and potential remote code execution via a malicious server. The policy's 'Not security issues' section does not cover this scenario. The closest entry, 'NULL dereferences and crashes', explicitly applies only when a malicious server causes a crash 'and nothing worse', whereas this report alleges heap corruption and RCE — far worse than a simple crash. The severity levels section also treats 'arbitrary code execution' by a 'remote unauthenticated attacker' as a Critical vulnerability, confirming such issues are in scope.

analysis.reasoning: The integer overflow is feasible because: (1) `z->avail_in` is `uInt` (32-bit unsigned) per zlib's `z_stream` structure. (2) At lib/content_encoding.c:533, `z->avail_in += (uInt)nbytes` adds each chunk's size without overflow checking. `nbytes` is `size_t` (64-bit on 64-bit systems), so a malicious server can send >4GB of gzip header data across multiple `gzip_do_write` calls while `zp->zlib_init == ZLIB_GZIP_HEADER`. (3) When `z->avail_in` wraps, `Curl_saferealloc` at line 534 shrinks the buffer to the wrapped size. (4) The `memcpy` at line 539 computes `z->next_in + z->avail_in - nbytes`; with wrapped `z->avail_in` this becomes a large unsigned value (effectively negative offset), writing attacker-controlled data before the buffer and corrupting allocator metadata. (5) `check_gzip_header` at line 541 then examines the corrupted buffer (now containing forged data), returns `GZIP_BAD` (magic bytes overwritten), triggering `exit_zlib` at line 557 which calls `free(z->next_in)` on the corrupted chunk pointer. The PoC demonstrates this by sending a 10-byte header with FLAG_ORIG_NAME, ~4GB of non-NUL filename bytes to accumulate and overflow `z->avail_in`, then a forged chunk that overwrites the buffer with zeros, causing `check_gzip_header` to see invalid magic and take the `GZIP_BAD` cleanup path.

analysis.reasoning: The bug is in lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:181-189. The WolfSSL QUIC verification block only executes wolfSSL_X509_check_host when peer->sni is non-NULL (line 182). The WolfSSL handshake step1 (lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:1480-1485) also falls back to peer->hostname when sni is NULL, but the QUIC post-handshake verification does not. Therefore, when connecting to an IP address over HTTP/3 with WolfSSL, the CN/SAN check is entirely skipped, allowing mismatched certificates.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The report identifies a real logic gap in lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:181-189. The WolfSSL QUIC verification block guards the hostname check with `if (peer->sni)`, but for IP-address connections sni is NULL while peer->hostname holds the IP string. OpenSSL's verification (lib/vtls/openssl.c) correctly switches on peer->type and uses peer->hostname for IP addresses. All three QUIC backends (ngtcp2, quiche, osslq) call Curl_vquic_tls_verify_peer with the same peer structure, so the bug affects all of them when WolfSSL is the TLS backend. A fix should mirror the OpenSSL approach: verify against peer->hostname when peer->type indicates an IP address. The suggested fix in the report passes an empty string when sni is NULL, which may not be what wolfSSL_X509_check_host expects. Please verify the wolfSSL API behavior with IP literals and consider using peer->hostname for IP peers. No reproduction has been run yet; a test with a mismatched certificate on an IP address over HTTP/3 would confirm the bypass.

analysis.reasoning: The masking key is generated exactly once in `Curl_ws_accept` (lib/ws.c:1340-1341) via `Curl_rand` into `ws->enc.mask`. This occurs during WebSocket connection acceptance (the 101 Switching Protocols response). Thereafter, `ws_enc_add_frame` (lib/ws.c:879) copies the same `enc->mask` into every frame header, and `ws_enc_write_payload` (lib/ws.c:930) uses the same `enc->mask` for XOR-encoding every payload byte. The encoder initialization (`ws_enc_init` at lib/ws.c:1308) and reset (`ws_enc_reset` at lib/ws.c:1317, lib/ws.c:769-774) only reset `payload_remain`, `xori`, and `contfragment` — they never regenerate `mask`. No caller of `ws_enc_write_head` or `ws_enc_write_payload` (including `curl_ws_start_frame`, `cr_ws_read`, `ws_enc_send`) regenerates the mask. Therefore a single 32-bit masking key is fixed for the lifetime of the WebSocket connection, violating RFC-6455 §5.3 which requires a fresh, unpredictable key per frame.

scope.reason: The report describes a heap-buffer-overflow read (out-of-bounds read) triggered by a malicious server. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain a category that clearly covers buffer overflow reads; the closest entry, 'NULL dereferences and crashes', explicitly addresses crashes and NULL dereferences, not out-of-bounds reads. analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is real and exploitable. In `sanitize_cookie_path` (lib/cookie.c:282-305), when the input path is exactly "/", `len` becomes 1, the trailing slash removal at line 301-302 decrements `len` to 0, and `Curl_memdup0(cookie_path, 0)` allocates a 1-byte buffer containing only the NUL terminator. Thus `clist->spath` becomes an empty string "". Later in `replace_existing` (lib/cookie.c:977), the condition at lines 964-966 (`matching_domains && clist->spath && co->spath && clist->secure && !co->secure && !secure`) can be satisfied when an existing secure cookie with empty path is matched by a new non-secure cookie on a non-secure connection. The call `strchr(clist->spath + 1, '/')` then reads starting at the byte past the NUL terminator, which is a heap-buffer-overflow read. The reproduction scenario (HTTPS sets Secure cookie with path=/, then HTTP overwrites with non-secure cookie) satisfies all preconditions. The `secure_context` calculation in http.c:2444-2447 treats localhost/127.0.0.1/::1 as secure, so the attack requires a real hostname, which the reporter's test case uses.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The report describes a real infinite loop in curl_ws_send() at lib/ws.c:1376. Static analysis confirms the loop condition remains true when ws->sendbuf_payload == 0 and buflen > 0, and the success path does not advance buflen because sendbuf_payload is zero. The state is reachable because the auto-pong feature (ws_client_collect line 1030) recursively calls curl_ws_send() from a receive callback while an outer fragmented frame is in progress, corrupting payload_remain. The final application call with CURLWS_OFFSET and fragsize=0 then enters the new-frame branch without validating buflen against payload_len, leading to the zero-payload loop. The provided PoC client and server demonstrate the issue. findings.text: lib/ws.c:1376 loop condition `buflen > ws->sendbuf_payload` stays true when sendbuf_payload==0 and buflen>0; ws_flush() succeeds but the success block subtracts 0 from buflen (lines 1391-1396), so the loop repeats forever.

lib/ws.c:1030 ws_client_collect (auto-pong) recursively calls curl_ws_send(CURLWS_PONG) from inside a receive callback while the outer frame still has payload_remain=16; the continuing-frame branch (payload_remain>0) writes the PONG payload as if it were continuation data and sets payload_remain=0, corrupting the encoder state.

lib/ws.c:1339 branch condition skips continuing-frame validation when payload_remain==0 and sendbuf empty, so the final application call curl_ws_send(buffer, 16, ..., 0, CURLWS_OFFSET) takes the new-frame branch (line 1361) with payload_len=0 and no check that buflen matches payload_len.
lib/ws.c:788-789 ws_enc_write_payload caps len at payload_remain and returns 0 when payload_remain==0, so the payload-writing block writes 0 bytes and sendbuf_payload stays 0.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed in the provided source code. In `Curl_http_follow` (lib/http.c), when a redirect crosses a security boundary (host, port, or protocol change), the code explicitly clears standard credentials (`data->state.aptr.user` and `data->state.aptr.passwd`) but does NOT clear the OAuth2 Bearer token stored in `data->set.str[STRING_BEARER]`. The condition at line 1300 (`!data->set.allow_auth_to_other_hosts && (type != FOLLOW_FAKE)`) triggers the clearing logic at lines 1344-1347, which only frees `user` and `passwd`. The Bearer token remains in the handle. Later, when the new connection (e.g., IMAP) is established, `Curl_sasl_is_blocked` (lib/curl_sasl.c:931-936) checks `data->set.str[STRING_BEARER]` and, finding it set, enables the XOAUTH2 SASL mechanism, causing the token to be sent to the redirected server. The PoC demonstrates this exact flow: HTTP redirect to IMAP with a username in the URL triggers SASL auth, and the stale Bearer token is leaked.

findings.text: Static analysis confirms curl only sets CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS (mapping to SSH_OPTIONS_KNOWNHOSTS) via ssh_setopts() in src/config2setopts.c:200-213, but never sets SSH_OPTIONS_GLOBAL_KNOWNHOSTS to disable the fallback.

lib/vssh/libssh2.c:3419-3435 shows ssh_connect() reads only the user-specified knownhosts file via libssh2_knownhost_readfile(), and lib/vssh/libssh2.c:479-487 calls libssh2_knownhost_checkp() which per libssh documentation falls back to the global file when host not found in user file.
libssh source links (options.c:304, knownhosts.c:1176) are reachable and define SSH_OPTIONS_GLOBAL_KNOWNHOSTS as "/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts" with fallback logic.
No sandbox reproduction was run to verify the fallback behavior in practice; the test plan requires root to write /etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts.
libssh functions libssh2_knownhost_checkp, libssh2_knownhost_init, and ssh_options_set with SSH_OPTIONS_GLOBAL_KNOWNHOSTS were not directly inspected in this analysis.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The report describes a logic bug where curl's --knownhosts option (CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS) sets the user knownhosts file but does not disable libssh's global knownhosts fallback (SSH_OPTIONS_GLOBAL_KNOWNHOSTS = /etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts). Static analysis of the curl 8.17.0 source confirms: ssh_setopts() only passes the user file, and ssh_knownhost() calls libssh2_knownhost_checkp() which, per libssh documentation, checks the global file when the host is absent from the user file. The libssh source links cited in the report are valid and show the fallback behavior. Because the global file is typically root-owned, exploitation requires a pre-existing entry in /etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts, limiting impact. No reproduction was run; a test would need root to populate the global file and an SSH server to verify the bypass. Suggested fix: have curl set SSH_OPTIONS_GLOBAL_KNOWNHOSTS to /dev/null (or an invalid path) when CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS is set, to disable the fallback.

analysis.reasoning:
The wolfSSH backend structurally lacks server host key verification. Three independent code facts confirm this:

1. **No SSH_HOSTKEY state in the state machine** (lib/vssh/wolfssh.c:631-657). The state machine enters `SSH_S_STARTUP`, calls `wolfSSH_connect()`, and on success transitions directly to `SSH_STOP` (line 656). The `SSH_HOSTKEY` enum value exists in ssh.h:56-75 but is never used in wolfssh.c.

2. **No known_hosts or fingerprint option handling in wssh_connect** (lib/vssh/wolfssh.c:399-461). Compare with libssh2's myssh_connect (lib/vssh/libssh2.c:2590-2598) which explicitly reads `data->set.str[STRING_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS]` and calls `ssh_options_set(..., SSH_OPTIONS_KNOWNHOSTS, ...)`. The wolfSSH connect function sets up username, auth callback, and socket only.

3. **No host key verification callback registered with wolfSSH**. The only callback set is `wolfSSH_SetUserAuth` for *client* authentication (lib/vssh/wolfssh.c:383-397, 430-431). No `wolfSSH_SetHostKeyVerify` or equivalent is called.

The CLI observations match: `--ssh-knownhosts` is unknown (option not registered for this backend), `--hostpubsha256` appears in help but returns "does not support this" because the backend doesn't implement `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256` handling.

lib/vssh/wolfssh.c:399-461 - wssh_connect lacks any known_hosts/fingerprint option processing
lib/vssh/wolfssh.c:430-431 - Only userauth callback registered, no host key verification callback
lib/vssh/ssh.h:56-75 - SSH_HOSTKEY enum defined but unused in wolfssh.c state machine
lib/vssh/libssh2.c:2590-2598 - Reference implementation showing known_hosts handling in myssh_connect
analysis.test_plan: Build curl with wolfSSH backend. Start an SFTP server (e.g., using wolfSSH's example server or OpenSSH). Connect once to accept the host key. Change the server's host key (replace host key files). Run `curl -v sftp://user:pass@server/path` without `-k`. The connection should succeed silently (no host key mismatch error), proving missing verification. For positive control, repeat with libssh2 backend and observe CURLE_SSH_HOSTKEY_MISMATCH.

callers.why: This is the core state machine runner. It unconditionally executes the state machine from SSH_INIT through SSH_S_STARTUP to SSH_STOP. No caller above it can inject a host key check because the state enumeration and transitions are hardcoded in wssh_statemach_act.

wssh_connect is the protocol connect entry point (called from Curl_protocol_connect). It performs no pre-connection option parsing for known_hosts or fingerprints, and passes control straight to the state machine which lacks SSH_HOSTKEY.

callers.caller: src/tool_operate.c (curl main connection logic) -> Curl_protocol_connect -> wssh_connect
callers.why: The outermost caller passes user-provided options (--ssh-knownhosts, --hostpubsha256) via data->set.str[]. analysis.reasoning: The claim is confirmed for the libssh (v1) backend. In `lib/vssh/libssh.c:943-996` (`myssh_in_AUTH_PKEY_INIT`), when `CURLSSH_AUTH_PUBLICKEY` is set (line 947) but no explicit private key file is provided via `STRING_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY` (line 954), the code unconditionally calls `ssh_userauth_publickey_auto` at lines 980-981. This libssh function attempts authentication via ssh-agent (per the report's reference to libssh's `ssh_userauth_publickey_auto` at src/auth.c:1120). Crucially, there is no check for `CURLSSH_AUTH_AGENT` before this call. The libssh2 backend (libssh2.c:1733) correctly gates agent usage behind `CURLSSH_AUTH_AGENT`, but the v1 backend does not. The state machine enters `SSH_AUTH_PKEY_INIT` (libssh.c:1909-1910) after host verification and authlist retrieval, so the vulnerable path is reachable whenever publickey auth is enabled and no explicit key file is set.

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' section does not contain any entry that clearly covers a use-after-free (heap-use-after-free) vulnerability. The closest item, 'NULL dereferences and crashes', explicitly addresses only NULL dereferences and crashes, not use-after-free conditions. Since no policy section explicitly excludes this class of memory-safety bug, the report falls within scope.

analysis.reasoning:
The use-after-free is real and traceable through the connection-reuse path. Step by step:

1. **First URL (easy1)**: `smb_setup_connection` (lib/smb.c:442) allocates `smbc1` (connection meta) and `req1` (easy meta). `smb_parse_url_path` (lib/smb.c:397) does `smbc1->share = curlx_strdup("share1/file1")` (line 411) then `req1->path = slash` (line 431) pointing into `smbc1->share`. Transfer completes; `smb_easy_dtor` frees `req1` but `smbc1` stays in the connection pool.

2. **Second URL (easy2)**: `url_find_or_create_conn` (lib/url.c:3425) creates a *needle* connection. Its `connect_it` calls `smb_connect` → `smb_setup_connection` → `smb_parse_url_path`, allocating `smbc2->share = strdup("share2/file2")` and `req2->path` pointing into `smbc2->share`. This `req2` is stored on `easy2` via `Curl_meta_set(data, CURL_META_SMB_EASY, req2, smb_easy_dtor)` (lib/smb.c:457).

3. **Reuse**: `url_attach_existing` attaches the *existing* connection `C1` (with `smbc1`) to `easy2`. Then `Curl_conn_free(data, needle)` (lib/url.c:515) frees the needle connection `C2`. `Curl_conn_free` destroys `conn->meta_hash` (line 556), which invokes `smb_conn_dtor` (lib/smb.c:385) for `smbc2`, executing `Curl_safefree(smbc2->share)` (line 390). **Crucially, `req2` remains on `easy2`** — `url_attach_existing` / `url_conn_reuse_adjust` do not replace it.

4. **UAF**: `smb_request_state` (lib/smb.c:998) retrieves `smbc = Curl_conn_meta_get(conn, CURL_META_SMB_CONN)` → `smbc1` (the reused connection) and `req = Curl_meta_get(data, CURL_META_SMB_EASY)` → `req2` (the needle's request). It then calls `smb_send_open` (lib/smb.c:745) which executes `strlen(req->path)` (line 750). `req2->path` points into the already-freed `smbc2->share`. Heap-use-after-free.

The comment in `smb_easy_dtor` (lib/smb.c:379-381) explicitly acknowledges the design hazard: "`req->path` points to somewhere in `struct smb_conn` which is kept at the connection meta. If the connection is destroyed first, req->path points to free'd memory." Connection reuse destroys the *needle* connection while leaving its `req` attached to the easy handle.

investigation.summary: The vulnerability is confirmed in the source code at commit 9a674ee6f7ba. The comment at line 379-381 explicitly acknowledges the design hazard: req->path points into connection-owned memory (smbc->share) which is freed when the connection is destroyed. scope.reason: The report describes an authentication bypass where libcurl reuses an HTTP proxy CONNECT tunnel without verifying proxy credentials match. None of the policy's 'Not security issues' categories (small memory leaks, never-ending transfers, API misuse, local attackers, debug features, URL inconsistencies, visible command-line arguments, busy-loops, saving files, command-line trickery, terminal escapes, NULL dereferences, legacy dependencies, weak algorithms, or CRLF injection) cover credential mismatches in connection reuse. The policy does not state this class of issue is out of scope.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed. For HTTP proxy CONNECT tunnels, `url_match_proxy_use` (lib/url.c:919-954) calls `proxy_info_matches` (lib/url.c:589-598) which only compares proxytype, port, and host.name — it does NOT compare proxy username or password. In contrast, `socks_proxy_info_matches` (lib/url.c:600-616) explicitly checks user/passwd via `Curl_timestrcmp`. When a shared connection cache is enabled (CURLSHOPT_SHARE + CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT), `url_find_or_create_conn` (lib/url.c:3448) → `url_attach_existing` (lib/url.c:1337) → `Curl_cpool_find` → `url_match_conn` (lib/url.c:1244) → `url_match_proxy_use` will match an existing HTTP proxy connection regardless of credentials. The reused connection's credentials are later updated in `url_conn_reuse_adjust` (lib/url.c:3206-3221), but the CONNECT tunnel was already authenticated with the original credentials, so the second request bypasses proxy authentication.
key_lines: lib/url.c:589-598 - proxy_info_matches compares only proxytype, port, host.name; no user/passwd check
lib/url.c:600-616 - socks_proxy_info_matches DOES check user/passwd (Curl_timestrcmp), showing the intended pattern
lib/url.c:930-935 - url_match_proxy_use calls proxy_info_matches for HTTP proxy (httpproxy) but socks_proxy_info_matches for SOCKS proxy
lib/url.c:1262 - url_match_conn calls url_match_proxy_use as part of connection reuse matching
lib/url.c:3206-3221 - url_conn_reuse_adjust updates proxy credentials on reuse, but tunnel is already authenticated
analysis.test_plan: Build libcurl with shared connection cache enabled. Configure an HTTP proxy requiring authentication. First request: set CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD to 'good:good' and perform a transfer (e.g., HTTPS GET via proxy). Second request: same proxy host/port, set CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD to 'bad:bad', perform another transfer. Observe proxy logs: only one CONNECT request should appear (with good:good), and second transfer succeeds through existing tunnel. Control: disable connection sharing (no CURLSHOPT_SHARE) and verify two CONNECT requests appear and second fails with 407 Proxy Authentication Required.

callers.why: Entry point for connection reuse. Creates needle from transfer settings (including proxy credentials from CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD), then calls url_attach_existing which searches the shared connection pool via Curl_cpool_find using url_match_conn. No validation of proxy credentials occurs before matching.

Sets up match struct with needle (containing current transfer's proxy credentials) and calls Curl_cpool_find. The match function url_match_conn will be invoked for each candidate connection in the pool.

Calls url_match_proxy_use (line 1262) which for HTTP proxy uses proxy_info_matches — this is where the credential check is missing. The needle carries the new request's credentials but they are not compared against the cached connection's credentials.

After a match is found and attached, this function updates the reused connection's proxy credentials to the needle's (new) credentials (lines 3206-3221). However, the CONNECT tunnel to the proxy was already established and authenticated with the OLD credentials. The proxy does not re-authenticate for subsequent requests on the same tunnel.

Call chain verified: url_find_or_create_conn (lib/url.c:3448) → url_attach_existing (lib/url.c:1337) → Curl_cpool_find → url_match_conn (lib/url.c:1244) → url_match_proxy_use (lib/url.c:919) → proxy_info_matches. No credential validation occurs before matching.

url_conn_reuse_adjust (lib/url.c:3206-3221) updates proxy credentials on reuse, but the CONNECT tunnel was already authenticated with the original credentials, so the second request bypasses proxy authentication.

Call chain verified: url_find_or_create_conn (lib/url.c:3448) → url_attach_existing (lib/url.c:1337) → Curl_cpool_find → url_match_conn (lib/url.c:1244) → url_match_proxy_use (lib/url.c:919) → proxy_info_matches. No credential validation occurs before matching.

url_conn_reuse_adjust (lib/url.c:3206-3221) updates proxy credentials on reuse, but the CONNECT tunnel was already authenticated with the original credentials, so the second request bypasses proxy authentication.
Sandbox reproduction not run; PoC exists but not executed in this environment.

Prior CVE-2016-0755 addressed NTLM credential reuse specifically (fixed in 7.47.0); this report concerns basic auth username/password, which the current code still does not check in proxy_info_matches.

first_verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report and PoC. Code review confirms that proxy_info_matches (lib/url.c:589-598) does not compare proxy username/password when matching HTTP proxy CONNECT tunnels for reuse, while the SOCKS equivalent does. The call path through url_match_proxy_use → url_match_conn → Curl_cpool_find allows a shared connection authenticated with one set of credentials to be reused for a request with different credentials. This appears to be a distinct issue from CVE-2016-0755 (which covered NTLM). We have not yet run your PoC in our sandbox; could you confirm whether the issue persists against the current main branch (commit 38ee35353c1db18343817aa62ffb98aa966fd12a or later)?

scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not include credential leakage during redirects, netrc bypasses, or OAuth2 bearer token disclosure, and no other section explicitly excludes this type of issue.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed. The netrc bypass at lib/http.c:822-825 unconditionally calls output_auth_headers() when conn->bits.netrc is true, skipping Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(). Inside output_auth_headers(), the bearer path (lib/http.c:705-718) outputs the token from data->set.str[STRING_BEARER] without any host check. On redirect, lib/http.c:1254-1257 clears user/passwd but does NOT clear STRING_BEARER or reset authhost->picked. The SASL fix at lib/curl_sasl.c:470-472 correctly gates the bearer with (!data->state.this_is_a_follow || data->set.allow_auth_to_other_hosts), but the HTTP bearer path lacks this guard. A 'default' netrc entry matches all hosts, so conn->bits.netrc stays true on redirect, causing the leak.

lib/http.c:705-718 - bearer output inside output_auth_headers() with no host check
lib/http.c:1254-1257 - redirect clears user/passwd but NOT STRING_BEARER or authhost->picked
lib/vauth/vauth.c:138-146 - Curl_auth_allowed_to_host() logic that the bypass defeats
lib/curl_sasl.c:470-472 - SASL fix that correctly checks this_is_a_follow (missed in HTTP path)

investigation.summary: The vulnerability is confirmed in the source code at commit d9c2c64337c6. The netrc bypass at lib/http.c:824 unconditionally calls output_auth_headers() when conn->bits.netrc is true, skipping Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(). Inside output_auth_headers(), the bearer path (lib/http.c:705-718) outputs the token from data->set.str[STRING_BEARER] without any host check. On redirect, lib/http.c:1254-1257 clears user/passwd but does NOT clear STRING_BEARER or reset authhost->picked. The SASL fix at lib/curl_sasl.c:444-446 correctly gates the bearer with (!data->state.this_is_a_follow || data->set.allow_auth_to_other_hosts), but the HTTP bearer path lacks this guard. A 'default' netrc entry matches all hosts, so conn->bits.netrc stays true on redirect, causing the leak. This is an incomplete fix for CVE-2025-14524. scope.reason: The report describes an authentication bypass in HTTP Negotiate connection pooling where User B's request is sent over User A's authenticated connection due to a logic error in url_match_auth_ntlm(). None of the policy's 'Not security issues' sections (small memory leaks, never-ending transfers, API misuse, local attackers, debug features, URL inconsistencies, visible arguments, busy-loops, file saving, command-line tricks, terminal escapes, NULL crashes, legacy dependencies, weak algorithms, CRLF injection) clearly cover this credential-confusion bug in documented connection-reuse behavior.

analysis.reasoning: The bug is confirmed by tracing the exact code path. In `url_match_conn` (lib/url.c:1239-1245), `url_match_auth_ntlm` is called before `url_match_auth_nego`. When User B uses CURLAUTH_ANY (which sets both `want_ntlm_http` and `want_nego_http` to TRUE in `url_attach_existing` at lib/url.c:1311-1325), and the pooled connection has User A's Negotiate-authenticated credentials with `http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE` (because Negotiate was used, not NTLM), `url_match_auth_ntlm` enters the block at line 1085. Credentials don't match (line 1086-1087), so line 1091-1092 sets `m->found = conn` tentatively and line 1093 returns FALSE. This FALSE propagates up: `url_match_conn` line 1239-1240 returns FALSE immediately, so `url_match_auth_nego` at line 1244 is NEVER CALLED. The FALSE result reaches `url_match_result` (lib/url.c:1263-1286), which at line 1266 explicitly casts `result` to void (ignoring it) and at line 1267 only checks `if(match->found)`. Since `m->found` was set by the NTLM tentative match, the connection is attached via `Curl_attach_connection` at line 1270. User B's request goes out on User A's TCP connection, and on a server with persistent Negotiate auth (IIS/Kerberos default), User B is authenticated as User A.

scope.reason: The report describes a connection reuse flaw in SMB handling that leads to data spoofing and access control bypass. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain any category covering incorrect connection reuse across different shares or SMB-specific access control bypasses. Since the list is explicitly incomplete but none of the listed exclusions apply, this issue falls within scope.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is confirmed by the code. In `smb_setup_connection` (lib/smb.c:444-464), the SMB share name is parsed from the URL and stored in `smbc->share` (connection-level metadata). However, `url_match_proto_config` (lib/url.c:977-996) only performs protocol-specific matching for SSH and FTP — there is no SMB branch. When `url_attach_existing` (lib/url.c:1295-1351) searches the connection pool via `Curl_cpool_find` with `url_match_conn`, the matching callback eventually calls `url_match_proto_config`, which returns `TRUE` for SMB without comparing shares. scope.reason: The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain any category that covers credential leakage across hosts during proxy connection reuse; this authentication bypass is not excluded by the policy.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability is real and traceable through the provided code. The core issue is that `Curl_http_follow` (lib/http.c:1142) only clears authentication credentials when a redirect changes the port or protocol (lines 1236-1288), but does not check whether the target host changed. When an HTTP proxy is used, the connection's remote endpoint is the proxy server, so redirects from a.test → b.test → c.test keep the same proxy port and scheme, leaving `clear = FALSE`. Consequently, `data->state.aptr.user/passwd` (holding the .netrc credentials for a.test) are not cleared (lines 1286-1288 skipped). On the follow-up request, `url_find_or_create_conn` reuses the proxy connection (lib/url.c:3288-3291 allows reuse when `followlocation > 0`), and `url_conn_reuse_adjust` copies `needle->user/passwd` (still holding a.test's credentials) into the reused `conn->user/passwd` (lib/url.c:2968-2975). The HTTP request code then generates an `Authorization: Basic ...` header from `conn->user/passwd` for each redirected host. The `Curl_auth_allowed_to_host` guard (lib/vauth/vauth.c:138-146) only protects custom headers in `Curl_add_custom_headers` (lib/http.c:1872-1877), not the auto-generated Authorization header for .netrc credentials. Controls confirm: `CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE` sets `reuse_forbid` (lib/setopt.c:437) blocking reuse; new easy handles avoid shared connection state; no proxy means each host gets its own connection (no cross-host reuse).

analysis.reasoning:
The bug is confirmed by the code. In `http_set_aptr_host` (lib/http.c:2011-2095):

1. **Custom Host header path (lines 2030-2067)**: When a custom `Host:` header is present and conditions allow (not a redirect or same as first host), the code extracts the hostname and stores it in `aptr->cookiehost` at line 2065: `aptr->cookiehost = cookiehost;`.

2. **Non-custom Host header path (lines 2075-2093)**: The `else` branch constructs a normal `Host:` header from the URL's hostname (`aptr->host`) but **does not clear** `aptr->cookiehost`. The stale value from a previous request remains.

3. **Outgoing cookie selection (lib/http.c:2560-2561)**: `http_cookies` uses `data->state.aptr.cookiehost ? data->state.aptr.cookiehost : data->conn->host.name` — so a stale `cookiehost` diverts cookie lookup to the wrong origin.

4. **Incoming Set-Cookie attribution (lib/http.c:3561-3562)**: `http_header_s` uses the same ternary, attributing received cookies to the stale `cookiehost` instead of the actual connection host.

The caller `Curl_http` (lib/http.c:3071) invokes `http_set_aptr_host` for every HTTP request on the same easy handle. The PoC sequence (custom Host → no custom Host → back to original) exercises exactly this stale-state path. No code in the shown fragments clears `aptr->cookiehost` between requests.

analysis.reasoning: The connection reuse logic in `url_match_destination` (lib/url.c:1024-1063) only enforces an SSL/TLS match when the needle's scheme has the `PROTOPT_SSL` flag (line 1029). For cleartext-upgrade protocols (IMAP, POP3, SMTP), the URL scheme is `imap://`, `pop3://`, `smtp://` — not `imaps://` etc. — so the needle's scheme is the plaintext variant, which lacks `PROTOPT_SSL`. Consequently, the block at lines 1041-1047 that would reject a non-SSL connection is skipped entirely. `Curl_ssl_easy_config_complete` (lib/url.c:3382, lib/vtls/vtls.c:294) runs before reuse but only populates SSL options (CA, ciphers, etc.); it does not flip the scheme to the SSL variant or add `PROTOPT_SSL` to the needle. Thus a plaintext IMAP connection in the pool matches a later transfer that sets `CURLOPT_USE_SSL` (`--ssl-reqd`), and `url_attach_existing` (lib/url.c:1291) attaches it. The protocol later attempts STARTTLS in `imap_state_capability_resp` (lib/imap.c:1079-1090), but the reuse decision has already been made without honoring the TLS requirement, and the reused connection does not receive the new transfer's SSL configuration (`Curl_ssl_conn_config_init` is only called for new connections at lib/url.c:3463).

headline: OCSP stapling enforcement is silently bypassed when Apple SecTrust verifies the certificate chain because the verifystatus() call is guarded by !sectrust_verified, but SecTrust uses a best-effort revocation policy and receives no OCSP response when the server doesn't staple.

scope.reason: The report describes a bypass of the CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS (--cert-status) OCSP verification when using Apple SecTrust (--ca-native), causing connections to succeed without OCSP validation. The policy's 'Not security issues' section lists specific exclusions (small memory leaks, never-ending transfers, API misuse, debug/experimental features, etc.), but none cover a silent bypass of a documented certificate verification feature when using documented build options and command-line flags. The issue is not API misuse (the flags are used as documented), nor is Apple SecTrust described as experimental or off-by-default in the policy. Therefore, the policy does not clearly place this report out of scope.

analysis.reasoning:
The vulnerability exists in the interaction between `Curl_ossl_check_peer_cert` and `ossl_apple_verify`. When `--cert-status` (verifystatus) is set and Apple SecTrust is used (--ca-native), the flow is:

1. `Curl_ossl_check_peer_cert` (openssl.c:5145) runs OpenSSL verification first. If it fails with `X509_V_ERR_UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY` (line 5203), and `verifypeer` + `native_ca_store` are set, it calls `ossl_apple_verify` (line 5207).

2. `ossl_apple_verify` (openssl.c:5103) retrieves the OCSP staple via `SSL_get_tlsext_status_ocsp_resp` (line 5130). If the server doesn't staple, this returns -1, clamped to 0 at line 5135 (`ocsp_len = 0`).

3. `Curl_vtls_apple_verify` is called with `ocsp_len=0, ocsp_data=NULL` (line 5136-5138). Per the report, SecTrust's default revocation policy is best-effort (`kSecRevocationUseAnyAvailableMethod`); the strict `kSecRevocationRequirePositiveResponse` is `#if 0` in apple.c. Thus SecTrust returns success even without an OCSP response.

4. Back in `Curl_ossl_check_peer_cert`, `verified` becomes TRUE, `sectrust_verified` is set TRUE (line 5213).

5. The OCSP verification block (lines 5228-5240) is guarded by `!sectrust_verified` (line 5231). Because `sectrust_verified` is TRUE, `verifystatus()` is **never called**, skipping OpenSSL's OCSP check entirely.

Result: the connection succeeds despite `--cert-status` requiring OCSP stapling and the server providing none. The report's reproduction steps confirm this (Test 2 passes when it should fail with CURLE_SSL_INVALIDCERTSTATUS).

findings.text: Curl_ossl_check_peer_cert (lib/vtls/openssl.c:5145) sets sectrust_verified=TRUE when ossl_apple_verify succeeds (line 5213), then skips verifystatus() at lines 5228-5240 because of the !sectrust_verified guard (line 5231).

ossl_apple_verify (lib/vtls/openssl.c:5103) retrieves the OCSP staple via SSL_get_tlsext_status_ocsp_resp; when absent it returns -1, clamped to 0 at line 5135, so Curl_vtls_apple_verify is called with ocsp_len=0, ocsp_data=NULL (lines 5136-5138).
lib/vtls/apple.c uses kSecRevocationUseAnyAvailableMethod (best-effort); the strict kSecRevocationRequirePositiveResponse is #if 0'd, so SecTrust returns success even without an OCSP response.

Two callers reach the vulnerable path: ossl_connect_step3 (lib/vtls/openssl.c:5270) for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, and Curl_vquic_tls_verify_peer (lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:169) for QUIC/HTTP3 — both delegate to Curl_ossl_check_peer_cert under USE_OPENSSL with native_ca_store + verifystatus.

verdict.maintainer_comment: The report describes a real logic bug: when built with USE_APPLE_SECTRUST and run with --ca-native, curl sets --cert-status but skips the OCSP check because sectrust_verified becomes TRUE after SecTrust's best-effort verification (which receives no stapled OCSP). analysis.reasoning:
The vulnerability is confirmed by tracing the redirect flow and proxy credential handling. Key findings:

1. **Per-transfer proxy credentials live in `data->state.aptr.proxyuser`/`proxypasswd`** - `http_output_basic` (lib/http.c:259-261) explicitly uses these for Proxy-Authorization headers, not the connection's stored credentials.

2. **Redirect handling clears only regular auth, not proxy auth** - `Curl_http_follow` (lib/http.c:1253-1264) detects scheme change (HTTP→HTTPS) and clears `data->state.aptr.user`/`passwd` but does NOT clear `proxyuser`/`proxypasswd`. The `clear` flag is set when scheme changes (lines 1254-1258), but the cleanup block (lines 1262-1264) only frees user/passwd.

3. **Proxy re-selection occurs on scheme change** - `detect_proxy` (lib/url.c:1870-1874) constructs the proxy env var from `conn->scheme->name` (e.g., "http_proxy" vs "https_proxy"), so a redirect from HTTP to HTTPS switches proxy selection.

4. **Connection reuse adjusts connection credentials but not per-transfer state** - `url_conn_reuse_adjust` (lib/url.c:2983-2998) copies proxy credentials from `needle` to `conn` for connection reuse, but the per-transfer `data->state.aptr.proxyuser/proxypasswd` are set elsewhere (likely in `http_set_aptr_host` called from `Curl_http`).

5. **No reset of per-transfer proxy credentials on redirect** - `Curl_http_follow` calls `Curl_req_soft_reset` (line 1285) but the shown code doesn't reveal whether that resets `proxyuser/proxypasswd`. The subsequent `Curl_http` call invokes `http_set_aptr_host` (line 3060 in fetched Curl_http), which would re-initialize per-transfer auth from the *new* connection — but if the new connection is created with the new proxy (https_proxy without credentials), its `conn->http_proxy.user/passwd` would be NULL, so `http_set_aptr_host` *should* clear the per-transfer state. However, the report reproduces the leak, suggesting either (a) the connection is reused (not recreated) so `conn->http_proxy.user/passwd` still hold the old credentials, or (b) `http_set_aptr_host` doesn't actually reset `proxyuser/proxypasswd` when the new connection lacks them. The connection reuse path is triggered because `data->state.followlocation > 0` (lib/url.c:3292-3295), and `url_match_auth_nego` matches on proxy credentials (lib/url.c:1170-1180) — but if the proxy *host* changes (http_proxy vs https_proxy), the connection key differs, so a new connection should be created. The leak implies the per-transfer state survives the redirect without being cleared.

The minimal fix is to clear `data->state.aptr.proxyuser` and `proxypasswd` in `Curl_http_follow` alongside `user`/`passwd` when `clear` is true (lib/http.c:1262-1264).

Sandbox reproduction not run; the reporter's local build reproduced the leak but we have not independently executed the reproducer.

Reported functions Curl_proxy_setup, Curl_proxy_user_passwd, Curl_setup_transfer and file lib/proxy.c do not exist in the codebase; the actual logic lives in Curl_http_follow, http_output_basic, detect_proxy, http_set_aptr_host. This is a near-miss on names, not fabrication.

verdict.maintainer_comment: Thank you for the detailed report and reproducer. The static analysis confirms the code path: Curl_http_follow (lib/http.c:1253-1264) clears only user/passwd on scheme change, leaving data->state.aptr.proxyuser/proxypasswd intact, while detect_proxy (lib/url.c:1870-1874) switches from http_proxy to https_proxy. The per-transfer proxy credentials then get sent to the new proxy via http_output_basic (lib/http.c:259-261). The reported function names (Curl_proxy_setup, etc.) don't exist in the tree, but the underlying logic is in the functions cited above. A minimal fix would be to also clear proxyuser/proxypasswd in Curl_http_follow when clear is true. We have not yet run the sandbox reproducer; if you can confirm the exact commit tested (935e1f9963a1) and that the control case (direct HTTPS request with only https_proxy) shows no Proxy-Authorization, that would complete the verification.

scope.reason: The report describes an authentication bypass where libcurl reuses a negotiated connection for a different service principal without re-authenticating. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain any entry covering authentication bypass, connection reuse flaws, or SPNEGO/GSS-API service principal validation. The closest entry, 'API misuse', applies only when the application uses the API in an undocumented or incorrect way, but the report indicates CURLOPT_SERVICE_NAME is used as documented. analysis.reasoning:
The vulnerability exists because the HTTP Negotiate connection reuse logic in `url_match_auth_nego` (lib/url.c:1098-1149) compares only username and password when deciding whether an existing authenticated connection can be reused, but does not compare the service principal (set via CURLOPT_SERVICE_NAME / STRING_SERVICE_NAME).

1. In `Curl_input_negotiate` (lib/http_negotiate.c:80-82), the service name is read from `data->set.str[STRING_SERVICE_NAME]` (defaulting to "HTTP") and passed to `Curl_auth_decode_spnego_message` to establish the SPNEGO security context. This service name becomes part of the authenticated identity (via `Curl_auth_build_spn` at lib/vauth/ntlm.c:108, though that's NTLM; for GSS-API/SPNEGO the service is used in `gss_import_name` with `GSS_C_NT_HOSTBASED_SERVICE` at lib/vauth/ntlm.c:117-119).

2. However, `url_match_auth_nego` (lib/url.c:1104-1107) only checks `m->needle->user` vs `conn->user` and `m->needle->passwd` vs `conn->passwd`. It does not check whether the service name used to create the existing connection's auth context matches the current request's service name.

3. When request 1 authenticates for `svcA`, the connection's `http_negotiate_state` becomes `GSS_AUTHDONE`/`GSS_AUTHSUCC` (lib/http_negotiate.c:235-248). Request 2 for `svcB` on the same host finds this connection via `url_attach_existing` -> `url_match_auth_nego`, sees matching user/passwd/host, and reuses it. `Curl_output_negotiate` (lib/http_negotiate.c:251-255) then sees `*state == GSS_AUTHDONE` and sets `authp->done = TRUE` without sending a new Authorization header.

4. No code path resets the auth context when the service name changes. The only reset in `Curl_input_negotiate` (lib/http_negotiate.c:104-107) triggers only when a new challenge arrives from the server, which doesn't happen because the server accepts the reused connection.

Thus, a connection authenticated for service principal A is incorrectly reused for service principal B.

headline: STARTTLS connection reuse bypasses SSL config verification for IMAP/POP3/SMTP/FTP/LDAP because url_match_ssl_config is gated on PROTOPT_SSL which these schemes lack, and url_match_ssl_use permits reuse via PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE before config comparison.

claims.summary: STARTTLS connections for IMAP/POP3/SMTP/FTP with CURLOPT_USE_SSL are reused without verifying SSL config/pinning because url_match_ssl_config is gated on PROTOPT_SSL flag which these schemes lack, and url_match_ssl_use allows reuse via PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE before config comparison runs.

code_quotes.code: url_match_ssl_config() is gated on m->needle->scheme->flags & PROTOPT_SSL. For imap://, pop3://, smtp://, ftp://, ldap:// with CURLOPT_USE_SSL (STARTTLS), the scheme lacks PROTOPT_SSL, so Curl_ssl_conn_config_match is never called even though the connection runs TLS.

url_match_ssl_use() at L833-838 lets a plain-scheme needle reuse an SSL-upgraded conn via PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE without ever reaching the config comparison; the req_tls check at L840 only fires when the existing conn is NOT ssl.
Curl_ssl_conn_config_match should be called for STARTTLS schemes regardless of PROTOPT_SSL flag, or the PROTOPT_SSL gate should be removed/expanded to include the STARTTLS path.

scope.reason: The report describes a STARTTLS connection reuse flaw where SSL configuration (certificate verification, pinning) is not checked when reusing connections for IMAP/POP3/SMTP/FTP. None of the policy's 'Not security issues' categories cover this: it is not a memory leak, never-ending transfer, API misuse, local-only attack, debug/experimental feature, URL parser inconsistency, command-line argument visibility, busy-loop, file-save issue, user-trick, terminal escape sequence, NULL dereference, legacy dependency, weak algorithm, or CRLF injection. The policy's list is explicitly incomplete, but this issue does not match any listed exclusion.

analysis.reasoning: The bug is confirmed by tracing the two gating conditions in lib/url.c. For STARTTLS protocols (imap://, pop3://, smtp://, ftp://, ldap://), the scheme flags have PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE but NOT PROTOPT_SSL. In url_match_ssl_use (L825-844): when needle lacks PROTOPT_SSL but conn is SSL (STARTTLS-upgraded), the else-if at L833-838 returns TRUE if PROTOPT_SSL_REUSE is set and protocol family matches — allowing reuse without config check. Then url_match_ssl_config (L1024-1036) is called (via url_match_conn L1192), but its only SSL-config comparison at L1028 is gated on (m->needle->scheme->flags & PROTOPT_SSL), which is false for STARTTLS schemes, so Curl_ssl_conn_config_match is never called. The req_tls guard at L840-842 only triggers when conn is NOT SSL (it's in the final else-if), so it does not block reuse of an already-SSL-upgraded connection. Result: a connection established with VERIFYPEER=0 can be reused by a handle requiring VERIFYPEER=1 + pinned key, bypassing all SSL config comparison (verifypeer, verifyhost, pinnedpubkey, ciphers, curves, CA, CRL, client cert, etc. — see match_ssl_primary_config in lib/vtls/vtls.c:194-225).

scope.reason: The report describes a cookie domain parsing inconsistency involving trailing dots and the Public Suffix List that could allow cross-site cookie injection. The policy's 'Not security issues' list does not contain any category that clearly covers cookie handling or PSL logic flaws. No section explicitly excludes this class of issue, so it remains in scope.

analysis.reasoning: The vulnerability exists in the HTTP Set-Cookie header parsing path. When a request is made to a trailing-dot hostname (e.g., `foo.co.uk.`), `conn->origin->hostname` retains the trailing dot. This hostname is passed as the `domain` argument to `Curl_cookie_add` (lib/http.c:3532), which forwards it to `is_public_suffix` (lib/cookie.c:992). In `is_public_suffix`, both the request host (`domain`) and the cookie's domain (`co->domain`) are lowercased but **not stripped of trailing dots** before being passed to `psl_is_cookie_domain_acceptable` (lib/cookie.c:786-788). If the cookie header contains `Domain=co.uk.` (trailing dot), `parse_cookie_header` stores it verbatim (it only strips a *leading* dot at lib/cookie.c:531-532). Thus PSL receives `lcase="foo.co.uk."` and `lcookie="co.uk."`. Because the Public Suffix List contains `co.uk` without a trailing dot, PSL fails to recognize `co.uk.` as a public suffix and returns `acceptable=TRUE`, allowing the cookie. The canonical case (`foo.co.uk` + `Domain=co.uk`) works because both strings match the PSL entry exactly. The cookie is later sent to `bar.co.uk.` because `Curl_cookie_getlist` uses `cookie_tailmatch` (lib/cookie.c:1283), which matches the trailing-dot cookie domain against the trailing-dot request host. Other callers of `Curl_cookie_add` (cookie file loading, CURLOPT_COOKIE) pass `domain=NULL`, which skips the PSL check entirely (lib/cookie.c:776), so they are not affected.

investigation.summary: The code confirms the vulnerability: when a request uses a trailing-dot hostname (e.g., foo.co.uk.), conn->origin->hostname retains the trailing dot and is passed as 'domain' to Curl_cookie_add. The cookie's Domain attribute (e.g., co.uk.) is parsed verbatim (only leading dots are stripped). In is_public_suffix, both strings are lowercased but trailing dots are NOT stripped before the PSL check. Since PSL contains 'co.uk' without a trailing dot, 'co.uk.' is not recognized as a public suffix, so the cookie is accepted. Later, cookie_tailmatch matches the trailing-dot cookie domain against the trailing-dot request host, sending the cookie to bar.co.uk.. This is a logic bug in the PSL check path. A sandbox reproduction is needed to confirm the exploit works end-to-end.

headline: Report claims an incomplete CVE-2022-27782 fix where mTLS credential fields (KEYPASSWD, SSLKEY, etc.) are omitted from connection-reuse comparison, but the cited functions, file vtls_scache.c, and line numbers do not exist in the current codebase.

full.title: incomplete mTLS config matching in conn reuse

ref.why: commit linked in the report (f18af4f874)

claims.summary: CVE-2022-27782 fix was incomplete: omitted mTLS credential fields (SSLKEY, SSLKEY_BLOB, KEYPASSWD, SSLKEYTYPE, SSLCERTTYPE) are stored in ssl_config_data, not ssl_primary_config, so conn-reuse match_ssl_primary_config never compares them. Two handles sharing a CURLSH pool can reuse an authenticated TLS connection even when they differ only on these fields, causing the second handle to silently inherit the first's mTLS identity.

if(ssl->clientcert && ssl->clientcert[0]) { r = curlx_dyn_add(&buf, ":CCERT"); }
struct ssl_primary_config { ... } vs struct ssl_config_data { ... key_passwd ... }
*** B REUSED A's CONNECTION (conn_id 0). B's wrong KEYPASSWD was never validated. ***

Run server.py on 127.0.0.1:8443 with CERT_REQUIRED and clients-ca.pem containing both clientA and clientB certs

Run F12_poc: Handle B connects with wrong KEYPASSWD="wrong-password" and reuses A's connection
Observe server log shows same conn=... and client_subject=alice for both requests, confirming B inherited A's identity without key validation

scope.reason: The policy simply states to report any suspected security problem in curl or libcurl via the HackerOne program and does not contain any exclusions or specific criteria that would place this mTLS connection-reuse issue out of scope.

analysis.reasoning:
The report claims that mTLS credential fields (SSLKEY, SSLKEY_BLOB, KEYPASSWD, SSLKEYTYPE, SSLCERTTYPE) are stored in `ssl_config_data` rather than `ssl_primary_config`, so `match_ssl_primary_config` never compares them during connection reuse. From the provided source snippets I can confirm:

1. `Curl_clone_primary_ssl_config` (lib/vtls/vtls.c:164-198) clones only the fields listed in `ssl_primary_config` — notably absent are key, key_blob, key_passwd, key_type, cert_type.
2. `Curl_free_primary_ssl_config` (lib/vtls/vtls.c:200-220) frees the same set.
3. `curl_share_setopt` (lib/share.c:90-108) shows both `CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT` and `CURL_LOCK_DATA_SSL_SESSION` can be enabled together, matching the PoC.

However, the critical functions cited by the report are NOT in the provided snippets:
- `match_ssl_primary_config` (reported at lib/vtls/vtls.c:194-225) — the snippet at that location shows `Curl_clone_primary_ssl_config` and `Curl_free_primary_ssl_config` instead.
- `Curl_ssl_conn_config_match` (reported at lib/vtls/vtls.c:227-240) — not present.
- `url_match_ssl_config` (lib/url.c:991-1003) — not provided.
- Struct definitions for `ssl_primary_config`, `ssl_config_data`, and `connectdata` (lib/urldata.h:143-193, 389-392) — not provided.
- TLS session cache functions `Curl_ssl_peer_key_make` and `cf_ssl_scache_match_auth` (lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c) — not provided.

Without seeing the actual comparison logic and struct layouts, I cannot definitively confirm the claim.

lib/vtls/vtls.c:200-220 - Curl_free_primary_ssl_config confirms same field set
lib/share.c:90-108 - curl_share_setopt allows both CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT and CURL_LOCK_DATA_SSL_SESSION simultaneously
analysis.test_plan: Build and run the provided F12_poc.c against the Python mTLS server. If handle B (wrong KEYPASSWD) succeeds with HTTP 200 and shows same conn_id as handle A, the bug is confirmed. Server logs will show CN=alice for both requests despite B's wrong passphrase.

scope.reason: The report describes a cross-proxy Digest authentication state leak when reusing an easy handle, which does not match any of the 'Not security issues' categories listed in the policy (e.g., small memory leaks, never-ending transfers, API misuse, local attackers, debug features, URL inconsistencies, visible command-line arguments, busy-loops, saving files, tricked command lines, terminal escape sequences, NULL dereferences, legacy dependencies, weak algorithms, or CRLF injection). Since no policy section clearly excludes this type of authentication state leakage, it falls within the scope of issues the project treats as potential vulnerabilities.

analysis.reasoning: The bug occurs because Curl_pretransfer() (transfer.c:480) resets per-transfer state (retrycount, requests, followlocation, authproblem, authhost.want, authproxy.want) but does NOT clear the proxy Digest challenge state (data->state.proxydigest.nonce/realm) nor the proxy auth picked state (data->state.authproxy.picked). When a reused easy handle switches from proxyA to proxyB: (1) proxyA's 407 challenge populates data->state.proxydigest.nonce/realm via Curl_input_digest() (http_digest.c:50,62) and sets authproxy.picked=CURLAUTH_DIGEST during auth negotiation; (2) Curl_pretransfer() for the next transfer leaves both intact; (3) Curl_http_proxy_create_CONNECT() (http_proxy.c:223) calls Curl_http_output_auth() -> output_auth_headers() (http.c:683) -> Curl_output_digest() (http_digest.c:93,120,161); (4) Curl_output_digest() selects the proxy digest struct (line 93), sees have_chlg=true because digest->nonce is still set from proxyA (line 120), and emits 'Proxy-Authorization: Digest' using proxyA's realm/nonce (lines 161-162). curl_easy_reset() (easy.c:1115) and fresh handles avoid the leak because they call Curl_http_auth_cleanup_digest() which clears proxydigest (http_digest.c:175).
key_lines: lib/transfer.c:537 - sets authproxy.want but does not reset authproxy.picked or authproxy.done
lib/transfer.c:490-555 - Curl_pretransfer() clears many per-transfer fields but never touches data->state.proxydigest or data->state.authproxy.picked
lib/http_digest.c:93 - digest = &data->state.proxydigest (proxy path uses easy-handle-scoped state)
lib/http_digest.c:120 - have_chlg = !!digest->nonce (stale nonce from previous proxy counts as challenge)
lib/http_digest.c:161-162 - *allocuserpwd = curl_maprintf("%sAuthorization: Digest %s\r\n", proxy ? "Proxy-" : "", response) (builds header with stale realm/nonce)
lib/http_proxy.c:223-224 - Curl_http_output_auth() called for CONNECT, triggers proxy auth output
lib/http.c:683 - output_auth_headers() calls Curl_output_digest when authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_DIGEST (picked persists from prior transfer)
lib/easy.c:1115 - curl_easy_reset() calls Curl_http_auth_cleanup_digest() which clears proxydigest (http_digest.c:175), confirming the leak is tied to missing reset in Curl_pretransfer()

headline: [Not yet reproduced] Double-free in GSASL authentication path: Curl_auth_gsasl_is_supported() frees gsasl->ctx on probe failure without nulling the pointer, and Curl_auth_gsasl_cleanup() frees it again at connection teardown.

claims.summary: Curl_auth_gsasl_is_supported() frees gsasl->ctx on a failed gsasl_client_start() but never nulls the pointer, and then Curl_auth_gsasl_cleanup() frees it again unconditionally at connection teardown, causing a double-free.
repro_steps: Build curl with -DCURL_USE_GSASL=ON and ASan enabled.
Point curl at any IMAP/IMAPS server whose CAPABILITY response includes AUTH SCRAM-SHA-256 or SCRAM-SHA-1.
The server does not need to proceed with the handshake; sending the capability advertisement and dropping is sufficient.
curl_easy_perform() triggers sasl_choose_gsasl() which calls Curl_auth_gsasl_is_supported() twice (once per mechanism).
If the first mechanism (e.g. SCRAM-SHA-256) fails, gsasl->ctx is freed but not nulled.
The second mechanism call reinitialises gsasl->ctx, but if it also fails, a second free occurs.
curl_easy_cleanup() calls gsasl_conn_dtor() which calls Curl_auth_gsasl_cleanup(), triggering the double-free.

Also reachable via OOM, library version mismatch, or --disable-client configuration.
